paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is a syndromic form of aortic aneurysm and dissection, with cardiovascular, craniofacial, cutaneous, and skeletal anomalies that overlap with Loeys-Dietz, Shprintzen-Goldberg, and Marfan syndromes (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015). Features include thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection, mitral valve disease, cleft palate, bifid uvula, hypertelorism, skeletal overgrowth, cervical spine instability, and clubfoot, with marked intra- and interfamilial variability (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015). Some patients with TGFB3 mutations have had short stature and others tall stature (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Kuechler et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a 9-year-old European-American girl, born to nonconsanguineous healthy parents, with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, and a failure of normal postnatal muscle development. At birth she had contractures of the right hand, most severe in the third and fourth fingers, and of all toes, a midline facial nevus flammeus, and mild hypotonia; birth weight was 2.9 kg (5th centile). She was evaluated for failure to thrive at 3 months. At 17 months she weighed 7.5 kg (less than 1st centile) and was 76 cm tall (5th centile), and had bilateral pes planus, mild pectus excavatum, hyperextensibility of multiple large joints, mild retrognathia, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, blue sclerae, and a bifid uvula with intact hard palate. Muscle bulk was decreased in all appendicular and axial muscles, with low tone, diminished reflexes, and markedly reduced subcutaneous fat. She stood independently with a positive Gowers sign at 20 months and walked at 24 months with a 'hip waddle' gait; neurocognitive development was appropriate for age. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. A quadriceps biopsy at age 7 years showed type 1 fiber predominance with mild, focal type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse. Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months showed no cardiac defect, and at 6.5 years the aortic root measured 1.72 cm (z score 0.39). The patient did not meet diagnostic criteria for Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, or Beals-Hecht syndrome, differing by significant growth retardation, absence of cardiovascular findings, and distinct muscle histopathology.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) reported 43 patients (23 male, 20 female; median age 34 years, range 3 to 74) from 11 families with syndromic aortic aneurysms. In a large Dutch family (family 1) with autosomal dominant inheritance, 7 members aged 40 to 68 years had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta; 3 died from aortic dissection and rupture. Four members had mitral valve abnormalities ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation requiring surgery. Craniofacial abnormalities were subtle, including long face, high-arched palate, and retrognathia; pectus deformity and scoliosis were frequent, and other findings included velvety skin, varices, hiatal hernia, and autoimmune features such as HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, and celiac disease. In the 10 additional families, vascular involvement ranged from no cardiovascular abnormalities at age 64 to type A dissection (median age 51 years, range 40 to 80) or type B dissection (median age 44.5 years, range 30 to 57), abdominal aortic dissection, and death from cerebral aneurysm dissection at age 55. Other cardiovascular features included mitral valve disease, persistent foramen ovale, and atrial or ventricular septal defects. No early arterial dissection, dissection at small aortic dimension, or striking arterial tortuosity was observed. Among the 43 patients, 12 had tall stature, 16 arachnodactyly, 14 hypertelorism, 11 bifid uvula, and 5 cleft palate; cervical spine instability, clubfoot, dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia, joint hypermobility, pectus deformity, kyphoscoliosis, and inguinal hernia were also observed. No ectopia lentis was found, and early-onset osteoarthritis was reported in 2 individuals. One patient had short stature and received growth hormone during puberty. The authors noted striking intra- and interfamilial variability. Histologic examination of dissected aortic wall from 1 patient showed elastic fiber fragmentation with increased collagen and proteoglycan deposition.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with low muscle mass, growth retardation, distal arthrogryposis, and features overlapping Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, Rienhoff et al. (2013) found no mutation in TGFB2, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, FBN1, or FBN2. Exome sequencing of the proband identified 2 heterozygous de novo changes: a nonsense mutation in CDH2 (c.208C-T, Q70X) and a missense mutation in TGFB3 (c.1226G-A, cys409-to-tyr; C409Y), the latter confirmed as de novo by Sanger sequencing. The concentration of N-cadherin in the patient's fibroblasts did not differ from controls, and the authors concluded that the CDH2 change was unlikely to be driving the phenotype, although modifying effects could not be excluded. The mutant TGFB3 ligand produced in HEK293T cells failed to activate a TGF-beta reporter, and in Xenopus embryos coinjection of mutant and wildtype TGFB3 RNA at a 1:1 ratio reduced pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signals to approximately 40% and 60%, respectively, without affecting BMP-mediated SMAD1 phosphorylation. Rienhoff et al. (2013) concluded that the mutation was hypomorphic, acting in a dominant-negative manner.

paragraphs.text: In a large Dutch family with syndromic aortic aneurysms in which sequencing of known TAAD genes had been negative, Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous splice site mutation in TGFB3 (c.754+2T-C) that segregated with the phenotype; cDNA analysis showed skipping of exon 4, predicting an in-frame deletion of 36 amino acids (glu216-to-lys251del). The mutation was also present in a 17-year-old family member without documented cardiovascular features but with mild systemic manifestations. Screening of TGFB3 in 470 additional probands with syndromic or nonsyndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm (350 by Sanger sequencing and 120 by exome sequencing) identified heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 further probands: 4 different missense mutations (D263H, R300W in 4 families, I322T, and L401P), a nonsense mutation (Y365X), and 2 single-base deletions causing frameshifts (L386Rfs*21 and N235Mfs*11). The Y365X mutation occurred de novo; the proband with this mutation also carried a SMAD3 variant of unknown significance that was present in his or her mother, who had variable connective tissue findings and mild cardiovascular involvement. All mutations were absent from control databases. On the basis of the truncating and in-frame splice site mutations, the authors hypothesized that the mutations result in loss of function of TGFB3.

paragraphs.text: In a father and his 2 children with tall stature, arachnodactyly, hyperextensible joints, hypertelorism, and bifid uvula, without cardiac or aortic involvement, Kuechler et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous c.898C-G transversion in the TGFB3 gene, resulting in an arg300-to-gly (R300G) substitution. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and segregated with the phenotype.

agent.process_note: Read in full the 2 full-text papers (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015), the abstracts of Kuechler et al. (2015) and Garcia-Castro et al. (2000), and the title-only record of Matyas et al. (2014). Garcia-Castro et al. (2000) is about N-cadherin and left-right asymmetry in chicken embryos and was not cited. For Matyas et al. (2014), only the title was available. I took its variant (R300Q, c.899G>A) and the patient's age from Kuechler et al. and Bertoli-Avella et al., and attributed those details to them. No reference data were supplied, so the TGFB3 MIM number is left out. The chromosome location (14q24) comes from Bertoli-Avella et al. Bertoli-Avella et al. did not give nucleotide changes for the missense, nonsense and frameshift variants, so those are listed by protein change only.
